headline: DeepSeek-V3 & Coder-V2: The Local Hardware Reality
summary: Deploying massive Mixture-of-Experts models locally flips hardware bottlenecks. While active compute stays lean, VRAM capacity dictates local feasibility.

slides.title: DeepSeek-V3 Local Hardware Reality
slides.subtitle: Can your workstation actually run modern open MoE models?
slides.body: Massive Mixture-of-Experts models promise frontier intelligence locally. But can standard developer hardware survive the staggering memory demands?
slides.deep_dive: Running open frontier models locally shifts the bottleneck from raw compute speed to memory bandwidth and multi-GPU interconnect topologies.
slides.key_fact: Total parameter footprint dictates VRAM capacity, while active parameters determine compute throughput.
slides.why_it_matters: Prevents engineering teams from misallocating hardware budgets on setups incapable of hosting multi-expert routing.

slides.title: Dense Models vs Sparse MoE
slides.body: MoE architectures activate only a fraction of specialists per token. Compute demands drop, but all weights must stay in fast memory.
before_items: Every parameter activates on every token
Compute scales heavily with model size
after_items: Dynamic routing activates selective expert subsets
Drastically reduced compute per generated token
Full parameter footprint must remain resident in VRAM

slides.title: The Hospital Triage Mental Model
slides.body: Think of MoE like a medical triage desk routing incoming patients to specific specialists. Only assigned doctors work, conserving energy.

slides.title: The Memory Footprint Bottleneck
slides.body: Without sufficient unified VRAM, massive MoE models suffer dramatic token throughput collapse when forced into system memory offloading.

slides.title: Host Workstation Constraints
slides.body: Standard consumer setups choke on high-parameter MoE architectures without strategic quantization and multi-GPU tensor sharding.
before_items: PCIe bus saturated by RAM offloading
Interactive generation grinds to a halt
after_items: Quantized weights fit in fast GPU memory

slides.title: Designing Workstation Clusters
slides.body: Engineering teams avoid costly enterprise clusters by combining dual high-VRAM workstation cards with high-speed peer-to-peer interconnects.
slides.scenario: A development team hosting internal code models needs low latency without sending proprietary code to third-party APIs.
slides.impact: Configuring efficient local MoE parallelism eliminates cloud subscription costs while guaranteeing zero data leakage.

slides.title: Local MoE Readiness Plan
slides.body: Evaluate your local infrastructure before deploying massive Mixture-of-Experts architectures into team engineering workflows.
items: Audit total pooled VRAM against full parameter sizes.
Verify PCIe lane bandwidth across all motherboard slots.
Test weight quantization to balance fidelity and memory.
Benchmark expert cache hit rates under concurrent load.

slides.title: Memory Capacity Trumps Raw Compute
slides.body: Sparse MoE flips AI hardware rules. You no longer need supercomputers for compute—you need vast memory capacity to hold specialists.
takeaways: Total VRAM determines whether modern MoE models run locally.
Sparse activation keeps inference fast once weights are resident.
Quantization and expert sharding make local hosting achievable.
